summary.text: For \(k\le 60\), explicit prime decompositions handle the finitely many cases. For \(k>60\), set \(n=2k+1\); the assumed nonzero determinant forces some matrix entry to be \(1\), yielding primes \(n+i-j\) and \(n+j-i\), whose sum is \(2n=4k+2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the sequence term in question. Thus, for each positive integer \(n\), define an \(n\times n\) matrix \(M_n\), whose rows and columns are indexed by \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\), by
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if both }n+i-j\text{ and }n+j-i\text{ are prime},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the displayed differences are nonnegative: since \(j<n\), we have \(j\le n+i\), and since \(i<n\), we have \(i\le n+j\). The sequence is
\[
 a(n)=\det(M_n).
\]

Assume the conjectured nonvanishing statement
\[
 \tag{H} a(n)\ne 0\qquad\text{for every odd }n>120.
\]
We prove that for every integer \(k>0\), the number \(4k+2\) is a sum of two primes.

First dispose of the finite range \(1\le k\le 60\). The following table gives, for every such \(k\), primes \(p,q\) satisfying \(4k+2=p+q\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|c@{\qquad}c|c@{\qquad}c|c}
 k&p+q& &k&p+q& \\\hline
 1&3+3&&21&3+83&&41&3+163\\
 2&3+7&&22&7+83&&42&3+167\\
 3&3+11&&23&5+89&&43&7+167\\
 4&5+13&&24&19+79&&44&5+173\\
 5&3+19&&25&5+97&&45&3+179\\
 6&3+23&&26&3+103&&46&5+181\\
 7&7+23&&27&3+107&&47&11+179\\
 8&3+31&&28&5+109&&48&3+191\\
 9&7+31&&29&5+113&&49&5+193\\
10&5+37&&30&13+109&&50&3+199\\
11&3+43&&31&13+113&&51&7+199\\
12&3+47&&32&3+127&&52&11+199\\
13&7+47&&33&3+131&&53&3+211\\
14&5+53&&34&7+131&&54&7+211\\
15&3+59&&35&3+139&&55&11+211\\
16&5+61&&36&7+139&&56&3+223\\
17&3+67&&37&11+139&&57&3+227\\
18&3+71&&38&3+151&&58&5+229\\
19&5+73&&39&7+151&&59&5+233\\
20&3+79&&40&5+157&&60&3+239
\end{array}
\]
In each row the displayed sum is immediately \(4k+2\). Every displayed summand is prime. This is a finite primality check: the distinct summands are
\[
\begin{gathered}
3,5,7,11,13,19,23,31,37,43,47,53,59,61,67,71,73,79,83,89,97,\\
103,107,109,113,127,131,139,151,157,163,167,173,179,181,191,193,199,\\
211,223,227,229,233,239.
\end{gathered}
\]
For each of these, primality follows by checking that it has no prime divisor at most its square root. Since the largest is \(239<16^2\), only the possible prime divisors \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) need be checked (with the evident adjustment when the number being tested is itself one of these small primes). Direct division gives no divisor. Thus the theorem holds throughout \(1\le k\le60\).

It remains to consider \(k>60\). Set
\[
 n=2k+1.
\]
Then \(n\) is odd. Also, because \(k\) is an integer and \(k>60\), we have \(k\ge61\), so
\[
 n=2k+1\ge123>120.
\]
Consequently hypothesis (H) applies and gives
\[
 \det(M_n)=a(n)\ne0.
\]

We now use the elementary fact that a square matrix of positive size and nonzero determinant must have at least one nonzero entry. Indeed, if every entry were zero, the matrix would be the zero matrix. Since its size \(n\) is positive, every term in the usual determinant expansion would contain a zero matrix entry, and hence its determinant would be zero, a contradiction.

Apply this fact to \(M_n\). There are therefore indices
\[
 0\le i<n,\qquad 0\le j<n
\]
such that
\[
 (M_n)_{ij}\ne0.
\]
By definition every entry of \(M_n\) is either \(0\) or \(1\). Thus this particular entry is \(1\). By the defining condition for an entry to equal \(1\), the two natural numbers
\[
 p=n+i-j,
 \qquad
 q=n+j-i
\]
are both prime.

It remains only to compute their sum and relate it to \(k\). The bounds on the indices ensure that both subtractions are exact in the natural numbers. More explicitly,
\[
 j<n\le n+i,
 \qquad
 i<n\le n+j,
\]
so neither expression is truncated at zero. We may therefore cancel in the ordinary way:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 p+q
 &= (n+i-j)+(n+j-i)\\
 &= n+n+i+j-j-i\\
 &=2n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, this identity can be seen by splitting into the two cases \(i\ge j\) and \(j>i\): in the first case, writing \(i=j+d\) gives \(p=n+d\) and \(q=n-d\); in the second, writing \(j=i+d\) gives \(p=n-d\) and \(q=n+d\). The index bounds imply \(d<n\), so the indicated differences are nonnegative, and in either case the sum is \(2n\).

Finally, because \(n=2k+1\),
\[
 p+q=2n=2(2k+1)=4k+2.
\]
Thus \(4k+2\) is a sum of the two primes \(p\) and \(q\) whenever \(k>60\). Combined with the explicit finite verification for \(1\le k\le60\), this proves that every \(4k+2\) with \(k>0\) is a sum of two primes, as required.
